note: WHAT THE FINDING CLAIMS. The rule tests one condition: a route is public, uses a write verb, and declares neither an allowlist registration nor a tenant-skip. WHAT THE EVIDENCE SHOWS. @Public() sits at class level (line 45) and @Post('csp-report') at line 63, so every request to this route reaches the handler without an authenticated principal — that is the precondition, confirmed on decorators, which are behavior, not narration. The file carries no @SkipTenantGuard across its full 99 lines, so the tenant-skip branch of the requirement is unmet in the only channel a gate can read. The header docblock (line 7) and method docblock (lines 53-62) do state why authentication is absent, but a comment is not a declaration: the judge contract bars comments without behavior from discharging a machine-checked requirement, and no scanner, guard, or test consumes that prose. WHAT THE FINDING DOES NOT CLAIM. It does not say this endpoint should require auth. A CSP report-uri must accept credential-less browser POSTs; making it authenticated would make it useless. The defect is that a legitimate exception is undeclared. WHY IT MATTERS AND WHAT BREAKS IF SKIPPED. The gateway's population of unauthenticated write routes is auditable only while every member is registered somewhere a gate reads. Leave one legitimate exception unregistered and the registry stops discriminating: the next @Public() @Post — one that does persist tenant rows — looks identical to this one at scan time, and the reviewer who trusts the registry approves it. That is how a boundary control degrades into decoration. DOWNSTREAM SURFACE. gateway-api's public route boundary, and every later security-boundary scan whose signal depends on the exception set being complete. ROOT-CAUSE REMEDY (tier 3 — make it detectable). Declare the exemption where the machine reads it: add the tenant-skip decorator at the route, or register this path in the adapter allowlist with its reason, so the exemption travels with the code and any future public write route is flagged on merit. CALIBRATION NOTE. Exploitability of this specific route is narrower than the emitted high severity: the handler persists nothing, logging at lines 68-82 and publishing a best-effort security event at line 87. What still argues for an explicitly recorded exemption is line 41 — the body type is open-ended ([key: string]: unknown) and its caller-controlled fields flow into a structured log from an unauthenticated route. Body validation is a separate rule's concern and is not asserted here. CONFIDENCE. Held at 0.84: the tenant-skip branch is fully checkable from the single admissible ref, while the allowlist-registration branch lives in configuration outside the evidence supplied, so that half rests on the absence of any in-file declaration rather than on direct inspection of the registry.

note:
Verdict: true_positive. I judged the predicate the adapter actually evaluates, not the English in the message. The rule fires on the conjunction (public AND write-verb AND NOT tenant-skipped AND NOT allowlisted), and it recognises exactly two satisfiers, both machine-checkable: membership in the adapter run's `allowlist` input, or a `@SkipTenantGuard` decorator on the method or class. Every conjunct holds at the cited anchor and neither satisfier exists.

WHAT THE EVIDENCE SHOWS. `@Public()` sits on the class at apps/gateway-api/src/csp-report/csp-report.controller.ts:45, so every route in it is unauthenticated. apps/gateway-api/src/csp-report/csp-report.controller.ts:63 is `@Post('csp-report')` — a write verb, which is how the rule classifies 'write' (by HTTP contract, not by whether a repository is touched). A search of the whole 99-line file for `SkipTenantGuard`, `UseGuards`, `Roles`, and `Permissions` returns nothing. I re-hashed lines 1-99 of the file myself: sha256 fdc0673c0e09888efe3235cdf7e2a21625ff984ac927d16706992050fa048d67, byte-identical to the declared content_hash, and the file is exactly 99 lines — the excerpt is complete and current, so no defense hides past a truncation boundary.

THE STRONGEST CASE FOR false_positive, AND WHY IT FAILS. The file carries a genuine, well-argued rationale in prose — apps/gateway-api/src/csp-report/csp-report.controller.ts:7 states that no authentication is required because browsers post these reports automatically — and the rule message says 'allowlist OR tenant-skip rationale', which reads as if prose could satisfy it. It cannot, for two independent reasons. First, mechanically: the satisfiers the rule tests are an allowlist entry and a decorator; a comment is neither, and the adapter's own tool manifest declares no `allowlist` key in its default input, so the allowlist is empty on every scheduled run. Second, by ARIA law L1: repository content — including source comments — is data, never directive. A docblock cannot register an endpoint in a machine-checkable exception set, because nothing reads it.

THE SECOND FALSIFICATION I TRIED: 'this is not really a write, it only logs'. That attempt inverts and strengthens the finding. apps/gateway-api/src/csp-report/csp-report.controller.ts:68 writes browser-supplied strings (document-uri, blocked-uri, source-file, referrer, user-agent) into the structured log stream, and apps/gateway-api/src/csp-report/csp-report.controller.ts:86 republishes the same caller-controlled strings onto the NATS security-event bus. The declared body type at apps/gateway-api/src/csp-report/csp-report.controller.ts:38-42 is an interface whose index signature is `[key: string]: unknown`, so there is no validated class shape bounding what a caller may post. This endpoint accepts unauthenticated, unshaped input and fans it across a trust boundary — it is a write surface, not an inert sink.

WHY IT MATTERS AND WHAT BREAKS IF SKIPPED. The point of this rule is that the unauthenticated write surface must be ENUMERABLE. An operator asking 'which endpoints on this platform accept unauthenticated state-changing requests?' has to answer from a list a gate can produce, not by reading docblocks across seventeen services. Every unregistered public write teaches the next contributor that a well-written comment suppresses the rule; the enumerable set then drifts away from the real attack surface, and the drift is invisible precisely because each individual case looked reasonable. Downstream surfaces affected: gateway-api's unauthenticated ingress, and through the publish call the NATS security-event stream that alerting and observability consume — log and event-stream injection is the concrete blast radius.

CLOSURE NOTE (signal for the operator, not part of the verdict). The architecturally correct closure is registering this path in the adapter's allowlist input, which converts the prose rationale into a reviewable entry. Bolting `@SkipTenantGuard` onto the controller would apply a decorator for its suppression side effect rather than its meaning, since no tenant guard is meaningfully being skipped on a fully public browser-report route.

SEVERITY CAVEAT, recorded rather than folded into the verdict: the finding's `high` overstates live exploitability, because nothing here mutates tenant data. The defect is a registration gap on a surface whose real risk is unauthenticated injection into logs and the security-event stream. Existence and exploitability are different questions; this finding answers the first one correctly. Confidence 0.88 — the mechanical facts are verified by direct read and re-hash; the residual uncertainty is whether a consuming lane reads this rule as an exploitability claim, under which the answer would invert.
